title: Former Alpine driver Jack Doohan received death threats over F1 2025 midseason replacement
content:
Former Alpine Formula 1 driver Jack Doohan received death threats heading into the 2025 Miami Grand Prix weekend, which is revealed in the latest season of Netflix show, “Drive to Survive.”

The Miami race would be Doohan’s final outing for Alpine, before he was replaced by Franco Colapinto. “I had six or seven emails saying if I am still in the car by Miami, all my limbs will be cut off,” Doohan said of the threats in “Drive to Survive.”

The Australian driver faced a lot of pressure ahead of what was his rookie season at Alpine, which ended after just six races. He had replaced Esteban Ocon for the 2024 Abu Dhabi GP, and during the 2024-2025 offseason, Colapinto was added to Alpine’s roster of reserve drivers.

The Argentine had a standout end to the 2024 season with Williams when he replaced Logan Sargeant. Colapinto was not signed to a full-time seat for the 2025 season, with Carlos Sainz being brought into Williams alongside Alex Albon. Other teams opted against bringing him in, before his deal with Alpine was concluded in January 2025.

Doohan then struggled throughout the start of the 2025 season – crashing during the first race, at home in Australia, and during a practice session in Japan a few weeks later.

There had been plenty of rumors circulating about whether Doohan would be replaced by Colapinto leading up to the Miami GP in May, rumors that Doohan and his former teammate Pierre Gasly discussed briefly in the “Drive to Survive” episode “Strictly Business,” which was filmed at the Miami race.

Gasly expressed on the show that he felt bad for Doohan because “everybody is talking about him in a way that is quite toxic.” The following scenes reveal examples of abuse Doohan had received and included him discussing the threats he received. “(People are) saying they’re gonna kill me here, if I’m not out of the car,” Doohan said.

In another scene, he said, “I was there with my f—ing girlfriend and my trainer, and I got three f—ing men, like, armed men. I had to call my police escort to come and get it under control.”

Alpine had put a number of security plans in place for the Miami event, including ensuring Doohan had a police escort.

In a statement supplied to The Athletic, an Alpine spokesperson confirmed the team was “aware of the threats in question ahead of the Miami Grand Prix” and that coordinated efforts with the F1 organization and the event promoter were carried out.

“The safety and security of all staff members, including drivers, is of the highest priority and is a matter the team takes very seriously at all events,” the Alpine statement continued.

An F1 spokesperson said in a statement, “Formula 1 is a family and a community that is based on respect and support for each other. There is no place for abusive behaviour either online or in person and the whole sport stands united against anyone that attempts to undermine our values. As a community and will report anyone found to be acting in this way to the appropriate authorities and platforms.”

The abuse Doohan endured was not an isolated incident in F1 2025. Then Red Bull driver Yuki Tsunoda was subjected to online abuse after he had a minor moment with Colapinto in a practice session during the Emilia Romagna Grand Prix weekend at Imola, which took place two weeks after the Miami round.

Tsunoda felt he was impeded by Colapinto and made a hand gesture in frustration during the incident. Colapinto did speak out that weekend, urging his fans to be respectful.

On the Monday after the Imola race, Alpine and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem released statements condemning the online abuse. The team said, “As an F1 team, we believe we are fortunate to be part of a global sport that evokes great passion and emotions, with an ever-growing community of fans who enthusiastically follow their favourite drivers’ every move, whether it be a brave overtake on track or what style they are sporting when they arrive in the paddock.

“We encourage everyone to remember that behind the visor of these superhuman athletes there is a person. An individual with feelings, family, friends and loved ones. As a team, we cannot condone online abuse and urge all fans of this sport we love, to be kind and respectful.”

The online abuse issue then escalated again as the 2025 season ended – this time in regards to Red Bull and Mercedes.

During the season’s penultimate race in Qatar, championship challenger Max Verstappen was leading the race, while points leader Lando Norris was making his way back up the field.

Kimi Antonelli was defending against the Briton but ran deep into a corner during the closing laps, which let Norris jump to fourth and gain points that would be important to his eventual title win a week later in Abu Dhabi.

Verstappen’s race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase and now former Red Bull adviser Helmut Marko made comments that suggested that Antonelli had appeared to let Norris past. The Italian driver was then subjected to so much abuse Mercedes said there was a 1,100 per cent increase in abusive comments compared to what it normally see on a grand prix Sunday

Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff later revealed that he and Lambiase “cleared the air,” while Marko apologised for the abuse Antonelli received.

Red Bull released a statement saying, “Comments made before the end of, and immediately after, the Qatar GP suggesting that Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli had deliberately allowed Lando Norris to overtake him are clearly incorrect.

“Replay footage shows Antonelli momentarily losing control of his car, thus allowing Norris to pass him. We sincerely regret that this has led to Antonelli receiving online abuse.”
